title: Composition
tagline: Planning, drafting and polishing essays in the descriptive, narrative, argumentative and reflective modes.

overview.intro: Paper 1 opens with a composition choice, and the mark scheme rewards three things above all: a clear controlling idea, organised paragraphs and accurate, effective English. This chapter treats the four modes the ISC prescribes — descriptive, narrative, argumentative and reflective — as four different jobs with different plans. You learn what each mode asks of its opening, how evidence and example differ across them, and how a plan of eight or ten lines prevents the commonest failure in the examination, which is an essay that drifts after its second paragraph. The chapter also covers the mechanics the examiner can see: paragraphing, linkers, tense control in narrative and the final read-through that catches slips.

facts.label: Four modes
facts.value: Descriptive, narrative, argumentative and reflective; the question paper offers a choice across them.

facts.label: Marks are split
facts.value: Content and organisation carry the larger share; language accuracy carries the rest.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: A 300–400 word target fits the time; a plan of 8–10 lines comes first.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: The composition is the single largest-mark question on Paper 1.

learningOutcomes: Distinguish the purposes and structures of the descriptive, narrative, argumentative and reflective modes.
Plan an essay quickly with a controlling idea, paragraph purposes and supporting details.
Write effective openings and closings that suit the mode and the question asked.
Control paragraphing, tense and connectives so that the reader can follow the argument or story.
Edit a draft for the commonest errors in grammar, spelling and punctuation before submitting.

learn.title: The four modes and the job each one does

blocks.text: A composition question is a request to perform one of four different jobs, and recognising which job you have been asked to do is the first mark. The descriptive essay paints a scene: it works through sensory detail and spatial order, moving the reader’s eye from one feature to the next, and its danger is a list with no shape. The narrative essay tells a sequence with a turning point: it needs a clear chronology, one central incident and a reason for the telling. The argumentative essay takes a position and defends it: it needs a thesis, reasons, evidence and an answer to the strongest objection. The reflective essay thinks aloud about an experience and what it revealed: it needs both the event and the thinking, in that order. Each mode therefore has its own plan, its own opening move and its own failure mode, and the fastest way to lose marks is to answer an argumentative question with a descriptive essay.

items: Descriptive: sensory detail, a spatial or chronological sweep, one unifying impression.
Narrative: chronology, one central incident, a turning point and a closing reflection.
Argumentative: thesis, reasons, evidence, rebuttal of the strongest counter-argument.
Reflective: the event first, then what it showed, with honest specific detail.
Read the question twice and underline the verb: describe, narrate, argue or reflect.
A mode mismatch — arguing when the question asks for description — caps the content mark.

items.text: Argumentative opening: “School uniforms should be abolished, not because comfort matters, but because uniformity of dress discourages the individuality schools claim to teach.”
items.note: The thesis appears in the first sentence and takes a position someone could dispute.

items.text: Descriptive opening: “The bus depot at six in the morning smells of diesel and wet concrete, and the light arrives in long pale strips through the roof sheets.”
items.note: Sight and smell establish the scene before any opinion enters.

blocks.caption: What each mode must contain
rows: restatement plus a warning or hope

learn.title: Planning in eight lines and choosing the opening

blocks.text: The plan is the essay’s scaffolding and it costs three minutes. Write the question number, then a controlling idea in one line, then a line for each paragraph saying its job and its two supporting details. That plan prevents drift because every paragraph has a stated purpose before a sentence of the essay is written. The opening sentence should do one of three things: state the thesis, drop the reader into the scene, or pose the question the essay will answer. Choosing the opening deliberately matters because the examiner reads the first two lines with special attention, and a memorised opening that does not fit the question is immediately visible. Finally, allocate the paragraph count: five or six body paragraphs suit most 300–400 word essays, and one idea per paragraph keeps the argument clean.

items: Plan: one controlling idea, then one line per paragraph naming its job and two details.
Five or six body paragraphs for a 300–400 word essay; never one paragraph per page.
One idea per paragraph; if two ideas arrive, they belong in two paragraphs.
The opening must suit the question; a memorised opening that misses the point costs content marks.
Reserve the last five minutes for reading the essay through for slips.

items.text: Plan for “Describe a place of waiting”
items.note: Central impression: patience under fluorescent light. P1 depot entrance (smell, light). P2 timetable board (flicker). P3 fellow passengers (posture, silence). P4 the arriving bus (relief). P5 closing image: the empty waiting room.
Thesis: no, but they should be redesigned. P1 examinations motivate revision. P2 they standardise comparison. P3 objection: anxiety. P4 answer: coursework plus timed papers. P5 restatement.

items.meaning: The single impression, point or thesis that every paragraph serves.
The sentence that states a paragraph’s job and links it to the controlling idea.
A connective such as however, therefore or meanwhile that signals the relation between ideas.
The moment in a narrative where the situation reverses or the decision is made.

learn.title: Paragraphs, tense control and the closing

blocks.text: A paragraph is a unit of thought, and its first sentence tells the reader which unit has begun. In argument, the topic sentence states the reason, the middle sentences supply the evidence or example, and the last sentence links back to the thesis. In description, the topic sentence names the feature and the rest renders it in detail. Tense control is the commonest mechanical failure: a narrative written in the past tense must stay there, and a habitual past — “every evening we waited” — must not slip into the present without reason. The closing should not introduce new material; it should return to the controlling idea, in new words, and leave the reader with the image or consequence the essay has earned. A summary paragraph that simply repeats the opening phrase word for word reads as padding.

items: Topic sentence first, evidence second, link back last — the shape of most paragraphs.
Keep one tense per time frame; switch only for a stated reason such as habit or quotation.
Avoid and then, and then: use meanwhile, thereafter, by dusk or a full stop.
The closing restates the controlling idea in new words; it adds nothing new.
Vary sentence length: a short sentence after two long ones carries emphasis.

items.text: Weak link: “Then he came. Then we ate. Then it rained.”
items.note: Three clauses of identical shape flatten the rhythm and hide the relations between events.

items.text: Strong link: “By dusk the argument had spent itself, and the rain arrived as punctuation.”
items.note: The varied shape and the figurative close give the passage a designed ending.

blocks.caption: Tense traps in the narrative essay

learn.title: Editing for the marks the examiner can see

blocks.text: The final pass is not a reread for ideas; it is a hunt for the errors examiners are trained to count. Read once for meaning and paragraph shape, once for verbs — every finite verb checked for tense and agreement — and once for the punctuation that carries sense: full stops, commas before conjunctions joining clauses, and apostrophes in contractions and possessives. Spelling trouble spots are predictable: words like accommodation, definitely and separate are frequently misspelt and frequently penalised. Diction matters too: very big, very sad and very tired waste the opportunity that enormous, desolate and exhausted would take. Finally check that the essay answered the exact question asked, because a beautifully written essay on the wrong topic still fails the content criterion.

items: Three passes: meaning and shape; verbs; punctuation and spelling.
Check every finite verb for tense control and subject–verb agreement.
Replace weak intensifiers: very big → enormous, very sad → desolate.
Common trouble spellings: accommodation, definitely, separate, occasion, beginning.
Last check: does the essay answer the exact question, in the mode requested?

items.text: Error counted: “The team are playing well and has won three games.”
items.note: Compound subject takes are and have; examiners count agreement slips explicitly.

items.text: Upgrade: “The very tired sentinel watched the gate.”
items.note: “Exhausted sentinel” costs no extra time and lifts the diction mark.

items.meaning: The choice of words, judged for precision and register.
The level of formality appropriate to the task and audience.
The quality of a text whose ideas connect so the reader never loses the thread.
The final read aimed at mechanical errors rather than ideas.

keyPoints: Identify the mode from the question verb before planning: describe, narrate, argue or reflect.
Write a one-line controlling idea and a job for every paragraph before drafting.
Five or six body paragraphs suit a 300–400 word composition; one idea per paragraph.
Openings must suit the question; memorised openings that miss the point lose content marks.
Keep one tense per time frame in narrative and signal any switch.
Topic sentence, evidence, link back: the shape of most strong paragraphs.
Vary sentence length; a short sentence after long ones carries the emphasis.
Replace very + adjective with the precise word the meaning deserves.
Proofread in three passes: meaning, verbs, punctuation and spelling.
The last line must answer the exact question asked, in the mode requested.
examFocus: Spend three minutes planning; a plan is cheaper than a rewritten essay.
The examiner reads the first two lines closely — make them perform, not announce.

Reserve five minutes to catch agreement, tense and spelling slips.

vocabulary.meaning: The single impression or thesis that every paragraph of the essay serves.
The arguable claim the argumentative essay sets out to defend.
The sentence stating a paragraph’s purpose and linking it to the whole.
A connective word or phrase signalling the relation between ideas.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best states a thesis for an argumentative essay on school gardens?
options: School gardens are nice to have.
School gardens should be compulsory in every urban school because they teach biology that no classroom can.
This essay will discuss school gardens and their benefits.
School gardens were common a century ago and have returned.
questions.answer: School gardens should be compulsory in every urban school because they teach biology that no classroom can.
questions.explanation: The keyed option takes a position, names the reason and could be disputed; the other merely comments.

questions.prompt: In a narrative essay, the turning point should appear:
options: In the first sentence so the reader knows the ending
After the situation is established, as the incident that reverses it
Only in the final paragraph, without preparation
Wherever the writer judges the moment most important
questions.answer: After the situation is established, as the incident that reverses it
questions.explanation: The turn needs setup to matter, and it belongs at the incident that reverses the situation, not at either extreme.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest opening for a reflective essay on failure?
options: Failure is a part of life that everyone must face.
I stood outside the rehearsal room holding a score I had not practised, and understood that the audition would go as my habits had decided.
In this essay I will describe my worst failure.
There are many causes of failure in modern life.
questions.answer: I stood outside the rehearsal room holding a score I had not practised, and understood that the audition would go as my habits had decided.
questions.explanation: The second opens inside the experience with concrete detail; the first states a cliché the essay will not earn.

questions.prompt: The closing paragraph of a descriptive essay should:
options: Introduce a new scene for completeness
Return to the controlling impression in new words
Ask the reader a searching question about the scene
questions.answer: Return to the controlling impression in new words
questions.explanation: The close returns to the unifying impression; new scenes and paragraph summaries both break the frame the description built.

questions.prompt: The sentence that states a paragraph’s purpose and links it to the whole essay is called the __________ sentence.
questions.explanation: The topic sentence announces the paragraph’s job, so the reader never loses the thread.

questions.prompt: The final check of a draft aimed at mechanical errors rather than ideas is called a __________ .
questions.explanation: A proofread hunts agreement, tense, punctuation and spelling slips rather than reconsidering content.

questions.prompt: Explain why a memorised opening paragraph can lose marks even when it is well written.
questions.answer: A memorised opening is written for a different question, so it will not perform the task this question sets. Examiners read the opening against the prompt: if it does not state the thesis, establish the scene or pose the question actually asked, the content mark suffers immediately. A memorised paragraph also tends to sit awkwardly against freshly planned body paragraphs, which exposes the recall and damages the coherence mark. The safer habit is to memorise structures — how a thesis or a scene is built — and write the sentences fresh each time so that they answer the exact question set.
questions.explanation: The content mark is set against the question asked, so an opening written for another prompt cannot earn it.

questions.prompt: Give two advantages of keeping one idea to one paragraph in an argumentative essay.
questions.answer: First, one idea per paragraph gives the reader a single reason to evaluate in each unit, so the topic sentence can state it plainly and the evidence can be gathered around it; the argument stays checkable. Second, it makes the essay’s structure visible to the examiner, who can see how many independent reasons support the thesis without rereading, which directly serves the organisation criterion. Loose paragraphs that mix two reasons force the reader to untangle them, and the mark for coherence falls.
questions.explanation: Coherence and visible structure are the organisation marks that single-idea paragraphs protect.

questions.prompt: Write a plan for a 350-word argumentative essay answering “Social media does more harm than good to teenagers.” Your plan must state the thesis, the paragraph jobs, two supporting details for each body paragraph and the closing move.
questions.answer: Thesis: social media harms teenagers disproportionately because its design amplifies comparison and fragments attention, though its connective value should be preserved. P1 — harms: comparison and self-image. Details: curated highlights; measurable rise in body-image anxiety studies report. P2 — harms: attention fragmentation. Details: notification loops; task-switching cost shown in recall experiments. P3 — objection answered: contact value. Counter: friendship maintenance real but passive scrolling displaces it. P4 — proposal: design regulation plus digital literacy teaching. Details: default time limits; school curriculum teaching attention habits. P5 — close: restate that the harm is design-driven and therefore fixable, ending on the consequence of inaction: a generation trained to compare rather than to attend. The plan keeps one harm or answer per paragraph so each topic sentence states one job.
questions.explanation: Fixing the thesis, the body jobs and the close before drafting is what prevents mid-essay drift.

questions.prompt: A candidate writes an argumentative essay whose body paragraphs each begin with a statistic. Identify the weakness of this technique and describe two repairs that would raise the essay’s marks.
questions.answer: The weakness is that statistics alone do not argue: a number without a warrant tells the reader what, never why it matters for the thesis, so the essay accumulates evidence without reasoning, and the content mark for development suffers. The first repair is to follow each statistic with a warrant sentence — a clause explaining what the figure demonstrates about the thesis — so that evidence and claim are explicitly joined. The second repair is to vary the evidence types: pair a statistic with a concrete example or an expert observation, because a mix reads as considered reasoning while a single register reads as a data dump. Both repairs also improve coherence, because each paragraph then moves figure, warrant, example, link.
questions.explanation: Evidence earns marks only when a warrant joins it to the claim; mixed evidence then reads as reasoning.
